lessons.title: The retrieval funnel
lessons.description: Why finding candidates is a problem of its own.
lessons.html:
Concept

A recommendation system cannot afford to run its most expensive model on every item. Retrieval uses a cheap score to find a manageable candidate set; ranking uses more features and computation to choose among those candidates. Eligibility determines which items can be shown at all. An auction can then combine predictions with bids and business rules.

Think of retrieval as deciding which applications reach an interview. A perfect interviewer cannot hire someone whose application was discarded earlier.

Worked example

Suppose there are 1,000,000 eligible ads. A ranker takes 0.2 milliseconds per ad under an illustrative serial assumption. Scoring the entire catalog takes 200 seconds; scoring 500 candidates takes 100 milliseconds. Real systems batch and parallelize work, but the computation still has to fit a serving budget.

If there are 20 relevant ads and retrieval returns 15 of them in its 500 candidates, Recall@500 is 15/20 = 0.75. Ranking can reorder those 15; it cannot recover the five missing ads. The meaning of "relevant" must come from a defined label or evaluation proxy, not just whichever score the retriever produces.

Application to this project

MovieLens provides user/movie feedback, so movies are stand-ins for ads. We learn a cheap embedding score and evaluate whether a user's held-out positive survives candidate generation. We do not have bids, impressions, or real auction labels.

Snap's public post describes the funnel. Covington 2016 shows a separate candidate-generation and ranking design at YouTube. Our implementation is an educational design choice based on public retrieval research.

Implement it

Before training anything, make a list of 100 toy item IDs and a separate set of five relevant IDs. Write a candidate generator that returns ten items and a ranker that reorders those ten. Measure relevant-item coverage before and after ranking. Keep the same candidates while changing the ranking function.

Then draw the full funnel and label which component your code represents.

Self-check

  • Can a ranker repair candidate coverage while keeping the candidate set fixed?
  • Why is a retrieval latency reduction useful even if ranking quality is unchanged?
  • What information would you need to define relevance for ads rather than movies?

Next: embeddings and two towers.

lessons.title: Embeddings & two towers
lessons.description: Turn users and items into a searchable shared space.
lessons.html:
Concept

An embedding is a learned vector representation. A two-tower retriever maps a query/user through one function and an item through another. Their score is a dot product. Because the item function does not depend on the current query, we can compute item vectors in advance and search them at request time.

The representation is useful when relevant pairs have larger scores than other pairs. Its coordinates do not automatically have interpretable meanings such as "likes sports"; rotations of the entire space can preserve all dot products.

Worked example

A user vector is [1, 0]. Three unit item vectors are [1, 0], [0.6, 0.8], and [0, 1]. Dot products are 1, 0.6, and 0, so the first item is retrieved first.

Without normalization, item [3, 4] scores 3 with this user despite pointing in the same direction as [0.6, 0.8]. L2 normalization divides [3, 4] by its norm 5. With both sides normalized, the dot product equals cosine similarity and vector length no longer affects ordering. That discards a possible signal; it is a modeling decision, not a mathematical requirement for retrieval.

Application to this project

An ID embedding table returns one trainable row per known user/item. The reference adds a learned linear projection to each side and normalizes outputs. The towers are separate functions, but this ID-only linear model remains closely related to matrix factorization. Side features and history modeling arrive in lesson 6.

For batches of B users and B items with dimension d, encoder outputs have shape [B, d]. U @ V.T has shape [B, B]: each row scores one user against every item in that batch. Serving uses [B, d] @ [N, d].T for N catalog items.

Implement it

  1. Reproduce the three scores above using NumPy or PyTorch.
  2. Build nn.Embedding(n_users, d) and nn.Embedding(n_items, d).
  3. Add separate linear layers, then F.normalize(..., dim=-1).
  4. Check output shapes and norms before writing a loss.
  5. Cache all item outputs; verify cached and freshly encoded scores match.

Compare with src/model.py. Read DSSM for shared-space matching and Koren for the MF connection in the paper guide.

Self-check

  • Why does feeding the current user into the item tower prevent one shared offline index?
  • What signal is removed by normalization?
  • Why can this ID-only item tower not sensibly encode a brand-new item ID?

Next: learning from negatives.

lessons.title: Learning from negatives
lessons.description: Teach the model what matches, one batch at a time.
lessons.html:
Concept

Training examples give positive user/item pairs. To make their scores meaningful, compare them with candidate alternatives. In-batch sampling uses the other items already in a batch, avoiding a fresh full-catalog score matrix at each step. These alternatives are unobserved items, not proven dislikes.

Softmax turns a row of logits into probabilities over its sampled candidates. With one positive, negative log probability rewards a large positive score relative to the rest. This is a sampled contrastive objective, not the exact full-catalog loss.

Worked example

Let one user's scores be [2, 1], with the first item positive. Its probability is exp(2)/(exp(2)+exp(1)) ≈ 0.731, and its loss is -log(0.731) ≈ 0.313. Divide scores by temperature 0.5: logits become [4, 2], positive probability becomes about 0.881, and loss about 0.127. A smaller temperature sharpens the distribution, but confidently wrong scores can produce larger losses and gradients.

Now let both columns represent the same positive item. Penalizing the second column as a negative contradicts the label. Our positive mask includes both:

loss(row) = logsumexp(all candidate logits)
            - logsumexp(positive candidate logits)

If all columns are positive, both terms match and loss is zero. Known training positives for the same user also enter the numerator. Held-out labels never do.

Application to this project

Popular movies appear repeatedly in batches, and users can have multiple observed positives. The mask avoids obvious contradictions, but cannot identify every movie a user would enjoy. Candidate sampling also favors popular items; lesson 5 explores it.

Implement it

  1. Calculate the two numeric losses above by hand and with tensors.
  2. Create a [B, B] matrix from the encoders and divide by temperature.
  3. Construct an item-equality positive mask; OR it with known training-positive membership.
  4. Use logsumexp for numerical stability; mask nonpositive numerator columns with negative infinity.
  5. Average row losses, call backward(), and inspect finite gradients.
  6. Run the duplicate-positive test, then compare against in_batch_loss in model.py.

Read Yi and Yang after implementing the basic loss; their correction mechanisms depend on the actual sampler and should not be pasted blindly onto this variant.

Self-check

  • Why can batch size affect training even with unchanged embedding dimensions?
  • Why is a declining sampled loss not proof of improving catalog recall?
  • Does changing temperature alone reorder fixed vectors during exact serving?

Next: evaluation.

lessons.title: Evaluation you can trust
lessons.description: Know what your metrics actually tell you.
lessons.html:
Concept

A split defines what information the model has and what future behavior it must predict. A candidate pool defines the alternatives it competes against. A metric only has meaning when both are stated. Strong baselines expose whether a complex model adds value beyond globally common items.

We use per-user training, validation, and test positives. Validation selects settings/checkpoints. Test estimates performance after selection; repeatedly choosing configurations based on test makes it part of model development.

Worked example

A user's four distinct positives arrive as A, B, C, D. Train on A/B, validate on C, test on D. During validation exclude A/B. During test exclude A/B/C. The held-out target remains eligible. An item can appear in another user's training data.

For three queries, top-2 predictions are [B,C], [A,D], [C,B] and targets are C,B,C. Two users have a hit, so one-target Recall@2 is 2/3. In this protocol it equals HitRate@2. With multiple relevant targets, recall needs a different denominator.

If a user has five eligible items, random Recall@2 is 2/5, not 2 divided by the original catalog size. Average this expectation across users when pool sizes differ.

Application: diagnose our measured first run

The saved five-epoch MovieLens reference has test Recall@100 of about 0.132, compared with 0.072 expected random and 0.274 popularity. Validation recall improved from about 0.087 at initialization to 0.144, while sampled training loss fell from about 0.609 in epoch 1 to 0.077 in epoch 5.

That supports learning relative to random, not superiority to popularity. Possible next hypotheses include the short schedule, weak ID-only representation, catalog sampling mismatch, and the positive-mass objective. None is established by this one experiment. See the measured output.

Implement it

  1. Hand-calculate the three-query example, then implement recall_at_k.
  2. Deduplicate user/item positives, split by per-user timestamp, and assert pair separation.
  3. Rank the full catalog, exclude seen items, and use deterministic tie handling.
  4. Compute popularity from training counts only; compare with expected random.
  5. Save validation metrics each epoch and evaluate the selected checkpoint on test.
  6. Add head/tail slices before changing the model. Compare with metrics.py.

Read the evaluation contract and Schnabel. Per-user chronology does not prevent cross-user future leakage; a separate global cutoff experiment is required for a deployment-like evaluation.

Self-check

  • How could a random baseline accidentally become too easy?
  • Why might popularity be a particularly strong MovieLens baseline?
  • Which claim would require multiple seeds or a fresh future evaluation period?

Next: ANN.

lessons.title: Approximate nearest neighbors
lessons.description: Trade a little search accuracy for a lot less work.
lessons.html:
Concept

Exact search scores every item and returns the largest scores. Approximate nearest neighbor search saves work by inspecting only promising regions or compressing representations. That introduces a speed/accuracy/memory tradeoff.

Flat search is exact. IVF groups vectors into coarse clusters and searches selected clusters. HNSW builds a navigable graph and explores promising neighbors. IVF's nprobe and HNSW's efSearch control search effort in different ways.

Worked example

Exact top-4 IDs are [3,7,2,9]. ANN returns [3,7,5,9]. Neighbor overlap is 3/4. If the user's actual held-out positive is item 7, both systems have target Recall@4 of 1 for that user. If it is item 2, exact succeeds and ANN fails. Approximation accuracy and recommendation quality answer different questions.

An IVF search probing one cluster may skip the cluster containing item 2. Probing more clusters can recover it at additional query cost. Searching every cluster in an IVFFlat index approaches exact scoring, though tie ordering can differ.

Application to this project

We export both towers' normalized vectors from one selected checkpoint and build indexes over the item vectors. On this small catalog, overhead can dominate. Performance numbers from a laptop and 1,447 items do not predict million-item latency. The reference exports storage size, not total resident or build-time memory.

Implement it

  1. Load the vector export and verify its model/embedding hashes.
  2. Build faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), add float32 item vectors, and search user vectors.
  3. Compare its top-K with a brute-force matrix product on a small fixture without ties.
  4. Build IVFFlat; train its coarse clusters before adding items. Sweep nprobe.
  5. Build HNSW and sweep efSearch; hold vectors and queries fixed.
  6. Warm up outside timing, measure p50/p95, and plot neighbor overlap versus latency.

Compare with src/ann.py and the ANN lab. Read Johnson/FAISS and HNSW; read ScaNN when adding quantization.

Self-check

  • Which changes improve the learned vectors, and which only approximate their search?
  • Why should index construction be outside query-latency timing?
  • Why must an index carry model version and item-ID mapping metadata?

Next: negative sampling.

lessons.title: Better negative sampling
lessons.description: Choose the competition your positives face.
lessons.html:
Concept

Training against sampled candidates changes the competition each positive faces. In-batch candidates reflect the interaction distribution, which often favors popular items. Uniform corpus sampling gives different coverage. Hard negatives are candidates the current model mistakenly scores highly.

Sampling correction, exposure bias, and hard-example selection are different problems. Correcting the candidate sampler does not make logged feedback representative of items that users never had a chance to see.

Worked example

Under a simplified sampler, item A has sampling probability Q(A)=0.5 and B has Q(B)=0.1. Equal raw training logits of 2 become approximately 2.693 and 4.303 after subtracting log Q. The less frequently sampled candidate receives a larger correction. These are corrected training logits, not a general recipe for changing serving scores.

If half your negative draws are uniform over N items and half come from q_batch, the marginal probability of a draw is 0.5/N + 0.5*q_batch(i). That alone does not settle how to correct the full loss: expected counts, repeated columns, positive inclusion, and the sampling process must also be accounted for.

Application to this project

Our v0 has duplicate and known-positive handling. Its multi-positive probability mass objective is not automatically the objective in Yi or Yang. Derive the assumptions of your extension, especially before adding a correction to every numerator/denominator column. Use a tiny catalog where full scores are affordable to check the behavior before a MovieLens sweep.

Implement it

  1. Count item frequencies using training data only; inspect the head/tail imbalance.
  2. Write a sampler that returns candidate IDs plus probabilities or expected counts.
  3. Derive your corrected training objective, including duplicates, on a three-item catalog.
  4. Test the uniform special case: a common correction to every logit should cancel in softmax.
  5. Add uniform corpus negatives at a fixed total candidate budget.
  6. Mine high-scoring unobserved items with a training-only checkpoint; mask known positives.
  7. Compare separate ablations for correction, mixture, hard negatives, and batch size.

Track overall and head/tail recall, epoch time, memory, and a qualitative audit of plausible false negatives. Read Yi, Yang, Facebook EBR, and the optional cross-batch paper in the guide. This phase is an exercise, not an implemented feature of the reference trainer.

Self-check

  • Why can a harder negative be a worse training example?
  • How does sampling without replacement change your probability assumptions?
  • Why can stale queued embeddings be problematic for cross-batch training?

Next: features and history.

lessons.title: Features & user history
lessons.description: Move from memorizing IDs to understanding intent.
lessons.html:
Concept

ID embeddings memorize behavior for known entities. Feature encoders can share information across entities: two movies may share genres even when one has few ratings. A history encoder maps a user's observed actions to a vector and can represent a user or session whose ID never appeared during training.

Pooling treats history as a set or bag. A sequence encoder can use order and recency. More complexity only helps if it adds useful information under a fair comparison.

Worked example

History item vectors are [1,0] and [0,1]. Mean pooling gives [0.5,0.5], which represents both interests equally. Weights 0.2 and 0.8 produce [0.2,0.8], emphasizing the second interest. Neither pooling rule distinguishes [A,B] from [B,A] unless the weighting mechanism uses position or time.

A sequence model with positional information can distinguish those orders. For a training target at time t, its input must stop before t. A causal attention mask prevents one position from seeing later positions, but cannot repair a data loader that already included the target in its history.

Application to this project

MovieLens genre flags can become a multi-hot content vector. An item tower might combine an ID embedding with a projection of genre features. A content-only path is needed for unseen items; concatenating an untrained new ID vector is not a cold-start solution. Track the original-to-contiguous item mapping when loading u.item; the baseline reference does not yet load genre features.

Implement it

  1. Extend data loading to preserve mappings and join genre flags to item IDs.
  2. Compare ID-only, genre-only, and ID+genre item towers.
  3. Replace user-ID lookup with a masked mean of pre-target training-history embeddings.
  4. Define padding and an empty-history fallback; test that padding does not alter pooling.
  5. Add learned pooling, then a causal sequence encoder with positions.
  6. Keep split, dimensions/budget, and evaluation policy comparable; report rare-item and heavy-user slices.

Read Airbnb embeddings and SASRec; PinSage is an optional graph extension. Record whether extra compute buys better recall instead of assuming it will.

Self-check

  • What does attention add if histories have no position or time signal?
  • Why must genre joins use a saved mapping rather than row order by assumption?
  • Can one user vector cover two unrelated interests without compromising retrieval?

Next: ads-style behavior.

lessons.title: The ads serving layer
lessons.description: Make good candidates eligible, fresh, and retrievable.
lessons.html:
Concept

A high score does not imply an item can be served. Eligibility can depend on targeting, budgets, policy, inventory, or geography. Cold start asks what to do without interaction history. Freshness asks how quickly a changed catalog or model becomes available to retrieval.

These concerns interact: new items need representations, eligibility can change faster than vectors, and a new model defines a different embedding space.

Worked example

An ANN query returns items [A,B,C,D]; only C and D are eligible, but K=3. Filtering that result leaves two items. Overfetching six candidates might find a third; prefiltering searches only eligible candidates but may require index partitions, filter-aware search, or more expensive work.

Suppose a held-out positive is ineligible. Counting its absence as a model miss confuses relevance with feasibility. Report both the proportion of targets that are eligible and recall among eligible targets, along with empty-result rates.

Now imagine item vectors were encoded with model v1 while queries use v2. Vector dimensions can match even when their coordinates no longer mean the same thing. A shape check cannot detect this; compatible model/export metadata is required.

Application to this project

Use genre categories and deterministic mock budgets as an eligibility exercise. These are simulations, not real ads constraints. Hold out complete items to test content-only cold start, rather than claiming a rare training item is unseen. For new users, explicitly serve a popularity/content fallback.

Implement it

  1. Define an eligibility function with query-time attributes and test edge cases.
  2. Compare exact eligible search with ANN+filter+overfetch; measure eligible recall and latency.
  3. Train a content encoder, hold out item IDs, and score their content without an ID lookup.
  4. Insert a newly encoded item into an index and measure time-to-retrievable.
  5. Persist model hash, preprocessing version, ID mapping, and build time with the index.
  6. Reject mismatched query/index versions; separately test insertions, deletions, and budget updates.
  7. Simulate exploration slots and quantify candidate displacement.

Read DropoutNet and Facebook EBR. The existing export checker in ann.py guards paired artifacts; a persisted serving index and these ads behaviors remain your implementation exercises. Exploration's online benefit needs a real experiment.

Self-check

  • Which changes require recomputing vectors, and which can be eligibility metadata updates?
  • Why can simply appending an item fail after changing the embedding model?
  • What should happen when fewer than K eligible items exist?

Next: production and transfer.

lessons.title: Production & transfer
lessons.description: Turn an offline result into a defensible decision.
lessons.html:
Concept

Offline retrieval estimates performance on a chosen set of observed labels. Online behavior also depends on exposure, ranking, auctions, fresh inventory, and user response. A randomized experiment tests a change under those conditions, subject to its randomization and measurement assumptions.

Transferring to another dataset tests a different boundary: whether the pipeline's data contract and model assumptions fit a new task. Reusing code does not require pretending query identity and evaluation are unchanged.

Worked example

Retriever B improves offline target recall from 0.25 to 0.28 but increases p95 latency from 20 to 45 ms. More candidates survive, yet serving timeouts or weaker downstream outcomes could erase the benefit. Decide in advance which success metric and latency guardrail would support shipping.

A conversion may arrive two days after its impression. An impression from an hour ago without a conversion is not necessarily a settled negative. Labels need an observation window and delayed joins keyed to the correct impression. Separately, features must reflect information available before the prediction, even if label construction uses later outcomes.

For transfer, a new OTTO session has no trained user-ID row. Its prefix history must construct the query vector. A MovieLens ID-only implementation cannot run unchanged on that query without defining a fallback or adapting the encoder.

Application to this project

You will write an experiment plan rather than deploy to real traffic. Then use one transfer dataset to stress the design. OTTO provides an official data/evaluation repository; H&M has a separate competition task. Internal candidate Recall@K and official competition scores must be labeled separately.

Implement it

  1. Write a one-page hypothesis with randomization unit, primary metric, guardrails, power/duration logic, delayed-label window, and rollback criteria.
  2. Sketch event schemas: impression ID, user/session, item ID, event/prediction time, model/index version, eligibility context, and eventual outcome.
  3. Specify a label join that avoids duplicated conversions and incomplete windows.
  4. Build a small OTTO or H&M adapter with query histories, targets, catalog, and time cutoffs.
  5. Run popularity plus a suitable learned baseline; preserve dataset-specific split rules.
  6. Report at least two failure modes that differ from MovieLens and explain required adaptations.

Read Schnabel for the logged-feedback problem and revisit the Snap post for the ML development cycle. Use OTTO's official repository for task definitions; consult H&M's evaluation page before reporting a competition score.

Self-check

  • Which assumption connects a logged offline metric to an online claim?
  • What makes a label delayed rather than a feature leaked from the future?
  • What would you measure before recommending this model to your future team?

Finish with the Phase 9 design walkthrough.

roadmap.html:
Plan for roughly 6–10 hours/week; adjust scope to understanding. The original PDF is preserved. This checklist corrects its leakage wording, baseline formula, and assumptions about guaranteed gains. Each phase ends with a measured result and a short experiment note. Use the reading guide for every named paper below. Start each topic with its concept-first lesson before opening the reference implementation or beginning the checklist.

Week Phases Deliverable
1 0–1 Funnel explanation and a five-epoch reference run
2 1–2 Your own v0, baseline table, and split audit
3 3 Flat/IVF/HNSW benchmark and tradeoff plot
4 4 Controlled negative-sampling ablations
5 5 Side features and history-encoder comparison
6 6 Eligibility, cold start, and incremental freshness demo
7 7–8 Experiment plan and a small transfer-data pipeline
8 8–9 Transfer report, reproducible results, system design walkthrough

Phase 0 — Understand the funnel

Read: Snap engineering, Covington 2016.

  • [ ] Draw eligibility → candidate generation → heavy models → auction from memory.
  • [ ] Explain what each stage optimizes and why ranking cannot recover a missed candidate.
  • [ ] Write five lines comparing retrieval/ranking objectives, model cost, latency, metrics, failure modes.
  • [ ] Identify scale, freshness, feedback bias, and calibration constraints in the source material.

Done when: give a 60-second explanation and distinguish documented public Snap behavior from assumptions in your learning project.

Phase 1 — Build and understand v0

Read: DSSM, Covington, Koren. Reference code is provided; rebuild it yourself.

  • [ ] Install dependencies and run five epochs on real MovieLens, with a saved log.
  • [ ] Trace positive definition, deduplication, ID remapping, validation/test holdouts.
  • [ ] Explain embedding dimensions, independent towers, dot product, normalization, temperature.
  • [ ] Hand-calculate Recall@K and a three-example multi-positive loss.
  • [ ] Explain unobserved negatives and duplicate-item/known-positive handling.
  • [ ] Sweep temperatures 0.05/0.1/0.2 using validation; record costs and metrics.
  • [ ] Compare against expected random and training-only popularity baselines.

Done when: reproduce the run and explain every step, including any failure to improve or beat popularity. Avoid promising monotonic metrics from five epochs.

Phase 2 — Honest evaluation

Read: BPR, Schnabel, Koren. See the evaluation contract.

  • [ ] Add an unnormalized dot-product MF/BPR or implicit-ALS baseline with its training objective documented.
  • [ ] Use identical candidate pools, splits, K, and seen exclusions for every model.
  • [ ] Assert held-out pairs are absent from that user's training; allow shared items across users.
  • [ ] Compare per-user leave-last-out with a separate global temporal cutoff protocol.
  • [ ] Report head/tail and light/heavy slices from training statistics, with sample sizes.
  • [ ] Isolate items with zero training positives; describe the ID-only limitation.
  • [ ] Append one baseline/results table and investigate the weakest slice.

Done when: one comparable table exists, with a concrete leakage audit and explicit vocabulary/catalog-time assumptions. Per-user chronology alone is insufficient.

Phase 3 — ANN retrieval

Read: Johnson/FAISS, HNSW, ScaNN. Runnable lab.

  • [ ] Export normalized item vectors; match Flat top-K against brute force.
  • [ ] Compare Flat, IVF, and HNSW on identical embeddings and queries.
  • [ ] Sweep nprobe/efSearch, then plot neighbor overlap versus p50/p95 latency.
  • [ ] Report held-out-target recall separately, serial QPS, storage bytes, and memory scope.
  • [ ] Add persisted index metadata and enforce model/index version matching at serving.
  • [ ] Measure scale effects rather than claiming MovieLens proves million-item performance.

Done when: benchmark table/plot and a deliberately mismatched version test exist.

Phase 4 — Negative-sampling improvements

Read: Yi 2019, Yang 2020, Facebook EBR; cross-batch negatives as an extension.

  • [ ] Derive the candidate sampling probability/expected count for your actual sampler.
  • [ ] Implement and ablate logQ correction in training, with the inference rule explained.
  • [ ] Mix uniform corpus and in-batch negatives; document the mixture and its correction.
  • [ ] Mine hard negatives using a checkpoint trained only on training data.
  • [ ] Mask known positives; audit plausible false negatives without claiming to know all of them.
  • [ ] Compare larger batches or a versioned cross-batch queue, including compute/memory costs.
  • [ ] Change one component at a time; rerun head/tail slices and report regressions.

Done when: separate rows isolate each change and you can explain which bias logQ addresses and which exposure biases remain. An improvement is not guaranteed.

Phase 5 — Features and user history

Read: Airbnb embeddings, SASRec; optional PinSage.

  • [ ] Add genre features to the item tower; retain the ID-only ablation.
  • [ ] Build a mean-pooled training-history user tower before attention.
  • [ ] Compare learned pooling with a causal last-N sequential encoder.
  • [ ] Ensure every history is cut off at query time; do not use future interactions.
  • [ ] Compare head/tail/cold items and light/heavy users on identical splits.
  • [ ] Inspect three multi-interest users and explain where a single vector loses coverage.

Done when: an ablation table and concrete qualitative examples explain what features/history helped. A session/history encoder is necessary for unseen OTTO sessions.

Phase 6 — Ads-style eligibility, cold start, freshness

Read: DropoutNet, Facebook EBR, Covington; Snap engineering for ads context.

  • [ ] Define mock category/targeting/budget eligibility using only available query-time data.
  • [ ] Compare pre-filtering with post-filtering plus overfetch; measure eligible recall and latency.
  • [ ] Hold out entire items from training and retrieve them from content features alone.
  • [ ] Give unseen users an explicit popularity/content fallback and test it.
  • [ ] Insert a new item's embedding without rebuilding the whole index; measure time-to-retrievable.
  • [ ] Allocate a small exploration share; measure candidate displacement in simulation.
  • [ ] Persist mappings/manifests and test stale deletions, budget updates, and model changes.

Done when: eligible results, cold users/items, incremental inserts, and mismatch rejection are demonstrated. Offline simulation cannot establish exploration's causal benefit.

Phase 7 — Production and experimentation

Read: Schnabel, Yi; Snap engineering.

  • [ ] Write one page on offline/online gaps: distribution shift, selection bias, stale vectors.
  • [ ] Draft an A/B hypothesis, randomization unit, success metric, and guardrails.
  • [ ] Choose run duration from power, traffic, delayed labels, and business cycles.
  • [ ] Sketch impression-to-conversion joins, event IDs, observation windows, and late labels.
  • [ ] Explain that popularity/logQ correction does not remove auction/exposure bias.
  • [ ] Predefine ship/iterate/revert rules and monitoring/rollback triggers.

Done when: the written plan makes a falsifiable decision possible. No production traffic or real experiment is required in this tutorial.

Phase 8 — Transfer to OTTO or H&M

Sources: OTTO's official repository, H&M competition.

  • [ ] Choose one dataset, review terms, and create a small reproducible subset first.
  • [ ] Map events, IDs, timestamps, and query histories into a documented data contract.
  • [ ] Adapt the user tower to sessions/history for OTTO; ID-only unseen sessions do not transfer unchanged.
  • [ ] Use a temporal split appropriate to the task and train-only preprocessing.
  • [ ] Re-run popularity/MF and retrieval baselines; document any architecture changes.
  • [ ] Report retrieval Recall@K and, separately, the competition's official metric.
  • [ ] Write one page comparing catalog scale, sparsity, query identity, and cold-start failures.

Done when: one transfer run reproduces from documented commands with honest baselines. OTTO's weighted multi-event Recall@20 and H&M's MAP@12 are not the same metric as our one-target Recall@100. Kaggle scores are optional.

Phase 9 — Onboarding preparation

Read: revisit the papers supporting each choice rather than memorizing titles.

  • [ ] Write a one-page retrieval design covering eligibility, towers, ANN, freshness, and metrics.
  • [ ] Explain recall/latency, dimension/memory, negative sampling, and filtering tradeoffs.
  • [ ] Reproduce results from a fresh environment and collect the final experiment table.
  • [ ] Give a ten-minute design walkthrough and name the largest remaining uncertainty.
  • [ ] Prepare questions: team-owned sources; bottleneck; training/negative sampling; offline-to-online evaluation; index/model freshness and compatibility.

Done when: your explanation is backed by your own measurements, and the repo makes it easy for someone else to reproduce them.

papers.html:
Read for one implementation decision at a time. These are supporting references, not claims that our small reference reproduces the papers' full systems. manifest.json has citations, phase mappings, and direct PDF URLs; references.bib is importable into a citation manager.

python scripts/download_papers.py
# Or download just the first implementation readings:
python scripts/download_papers.py --only youtube-2016 yi-logq-2019

The downloader validates PDF headers, caches files in papers/pdfs/, records SHA-256 hashes in downloads.json, and reports failures explicitly. PDFs remain local; original author/publisher links and the downloader are versioned. Original copyrights and source-specific terms apply. DSSM, Airbnb, and MF have source/DOI links rather than automatic PDF downloads. Microsoft's currently linked DSSM PDF is a talk deck, so it is not mislabeled as the full paper here.

Read first: Snap's public context

Machine Learning for Snapchat Ad Ranking (Snap Engineering, February 11, 2022). Phase 0 and 7. Use the post to understand eligibility, candidate generation, heavy models, auction, and feedback. It is a dated public description; verify present team-specific architecture during onboarding.

Core reading order

  1. Covington, Adams, Sargin — Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations (RecSys 2016). Source · PDF · DOI 10.1145/2959100.2959190. Phases 0–1, 6. Read for separating candidate generation from ranking. Exercise: draw where offline item-vector computation saves serving work.

  2. Huang et al. — Learning Deep Structured Semantic Models for Web Search using Clickthrough Data (CIKM 2013). Microsoft source · DOI 10.1145/2505515.2505665. Phase 1. Read for a shared semantic space and query/document encoders. Exercise: distinguish its text features from our ID embeddings.

  3. Yi et al. — Sampling-Bias-Corrected Neural Modeling for Large Corpus Item Recommendations (RecSys 2019). Source · PDF · DOI 10.1145/3298689.3346996. Phase 4. Read for the candidate sampling distribution. Exercise: derive your sampler's correction before coding it; separate sampling bias from exposure bias.

  4. Yang et al. — Mixed Negative Sampling for Learning Two-tower Neural Networks in Recommendations (WWW Companion 2020). Source · PDF · DOI 10.1145/3366424.3386195. Phase 4. Read for combining batch and uniform negatives. Exercise: compare mixtures at a fixed total negative budget.

  5. Jui-Ting Huang et al. — Embedding-based Retrieval in Facebook Search (KDD 2020). Source · PDF · DOI 10.1145/3394486.3403305. Phases 4, 6. Read for end-to-end retrieval modeling and serving tradeoffs. Exercise: identify model and index choices that must be evaluated jointly.

  6. Johnson, Douze, Jégou — Billion-scale Similarity Search with GPUs (IEEE Transactions on Big Data 2019; preprint 2017). Source · PDF · DOI 10.1109/TBDATA.2019.2921572. Phase 3. Read for scalable vector search. Exercise: compare Flat with IVF; our CPU lab does not reproduce the paper's GPU performance.

  7. Guo et al. — Accelerating Large-Scale Inference with Anisotropic Vector Quantization (ICML 2020). Source · PDF. Phase 3 extension. Read for quantization objectives aligned with inner product. Exercise: explain why vector reconstruction error need not preserve top-K.

  8. Kang, McAuley — Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation (ICDM 2018). Source · PDF. Phase 5. Read for causal history modeling. Exercise: compare causal attention against mean pooling on the same histories.

  9. Grbovic, Cheng — Real-time Personalization using Embeddings for Search Ranking at Airbnb (KDD 2018). Conference source · Airbnb publication index · DOI 10.1145/3219819.3219885. Phase 5. Read for embeddings from marketplace behavior. Exercise: identify what short-term intent an ID-only user tower misses.

  10. Schnabel et al. — Recommendations as Treatments: Debiasing Learning and Evaluation (ICML 2016). Source · PDF. Phases 2, 7; read early when auditing evaluation. Exercise: explain what propensity information would be needed before claiming unbiased offline estimates.

Supporting and extension papers

Reference Source / PDF Phase and implementation question
Koren, Bell, Volinsky. Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems. Computer 42(8), 30–37, 2009. DOI 1–2: what does a linear two-tower add beyond dot-product MF?
Rendle et al. BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback. UAI 2009. Source / PDF 2: compare pairwise and in-batch training objectives.
Malkov, Yashunin. Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs. IEEE TPAMI 42(4), 2020; preprint 2016. Source / PDF 3: sweep graph search effort and measure neighbor overlap/latency.
Ying et al. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks for Web-Scale Recommender Systems. KDD 2018. Source / PDF 5 extension: when might graph context help item features?
Volkovs, Yu, Poutanen. DropoutNet: Addressing Cold Start in Recommender Systems. NeurIPS 2017. Source / PDF 6: simulate missing interaction information during training.
Wang, Zhu, He. Cross-Batch Negative Sampling for Training Two-Tower Recommenders. SIGIR 2021. Source / PDF 4 extension: what happens when queued embeddings become stale?

The core sequence follows your PDF. You can read FAISS/HNSW before negative sampling to match the implementation schedule. Papers are not strict prerequisites for each other. Read the relevant method and evaluation sections when a task needs them.

A note template for every paper

Copy this into your experiment note: problem; training examples; score function; loss/sampler; serving assumptions; evaluation; one idea to implement; one caveat. Finish with a falsifiable prediction for your own experiment.

start.html:
Budget: two or three focused sessions. Read the README setup first.

1. Run the reference

  • [ ] Run python -m pytest -q.
  • [ ] Run python -m src.train --epochs 5 --output artifacts/first-run.
  • [ ] Read config.json: confirm MovieLens, rating threshold, seed, and split hash.
  • [ ] Read all epoch lines and metrics.json; compare epoch 0 and the best validation epoch.
  • [ ] Copy validation metrics and baselines into results/experiments.csv.
  • [ ] Explain any regression instead of changing the test split.

Artifacts: config.json, metrics.json, model.pt, embeddings.npz, manifest.json. The trained checkpoint corresponds to the best validation epoch, not necessarily the last epoch. Baselines share the same candidate pool and split.

2. Explain the math with a three-example batch

For user vectors U and item vectors V, both [B, d], scores are S = U @ V.T / temperature, shape [B, B]. A row is one retrieval query.

  • [ ] Draw the 3×3 matrix and identify positive columns.
  • [ ] Explain why unobserved items may be false negatives.
  • [ ] Use item IDs [7, 7, 9]; show why diagonal-only cross entropy is wrong here.
  • [ ] Explain the reference loss: logsumexp(all) - logsumexp(positives) per row.
  • [ ] Show how known training positives enter the mask; explain why validation/test labels cannot.
  • [ ] Explain that normalized dot product is cosine; normalization removes norm information.
  • [ ] Explain how temperature scales logits and gradients; it does not change exact serving order for fixed vectors.

Normalization is a modeling choice, not a universal retrieval requirement. Without it, maximum inner product search can use vector norms as a signal. Our sampled contrastive objective approximates a retrieval learning task; it is not exact full-catalog softmax, nor a reproduction of DSSM or YouTube.

3. Rebuild the pieces yourself

git switch -c learn/v0

Create scratch/ and implement in this order, using the reference only to check:

  1. Load positive rows, deduplicate user/item pairs, remap IDs, split each user by timestamp.
  2. Hand-compute top-2 and Recall@2 on four items. Then implement full-catalog evaluation.
  3. Create an embedding and projection for each tower; check output shapes and norms.
  4. Implement the multi-positive loss using logsumexp. Backpropagate one batch.
  5. Shuffle training pairs, optimize with Adam, evaluate validation, save the best checkpoint.

Do not delete the reference to get started. Compare outputs on the same tiny fixture, then run your implementation on the fixed MovieLens split.

4. Do one controlled experiment

  • [ ] Run temperatures 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 with identical seed, dimensions, batch size, and epochs.
  • [ ] Use a unique output directory for each run.
  • [ ] Select by validation and explain your decision; reserve a fresh future split for unbiased final claims after repeated experimentation.
  • [ ] Write five sentences: result, baseline, hypothesis, cost, next experiment.

Done when: you can trace one batch from events to loss, reproduce the metric by hand, describe the validation/test distinction, and explain the baseline comparison. Expected trends are hypotheses to check, not guaranteed acceptance thresholds.

Read alongside: YouTube, DSSM, and the evaluation note. Leave logQ and hard negatives for Phase 4.

evaluation.html:
Current protocol

MovieLens-100k ratings ≥4 count as positive feedback. Lower ratings are unused, not explicit negatives. Keep the earliest positive per user/item, discard users with fewer than three distinct positives, sort by timestamp then item ID, and hold out the last two positives per user for validation/test. IDs are remapped over the retained catalog, so items with no training positives can exist.

Validation filters that user's training positives. Test filters training and validation positives. The model is not retrained on validation. For every query, the held-out target must remain eligible. The same movie may be in training for other users; that is expected collaborative learning, not pair leakage.

This protocol is chronological within each user only. Other users' training events can occur after a user's evaluation time. It therefore does not establish global temporal safety. Phase 2 requires a global cutoff experiment, train-only feature statistics, a catalog available at query time, and explicit cold-user/item policies before making a deployment-like claim. Even the catalog definition is an assumption here; validation/test metadata informs the remapped vocabulary.

Metrics

With one target per user, Recall@K equals HitRate@K: mean(target is present among the first K eligible predictions). It is not precision, CTR, or a calibrated conversion probability. Scores are computed against the full retained catalog, not sampled distractors. Ties break by catalog ID. Excluded slots are padded with -1 if necessary.

The exact expected random recall is mean(min(K / eligible_catalog_size_for_user, 1)). K / n_items only applies to an unfiltered catalog with K ≤ n_items. Popularity counts come from training only. Its test and validation metrics use the same exclusions as the learned model. Test scores from repeated runs can influence human choices; do not call the resulting model selection unbiased.

Training assumptions

In-batch candidates follow the training interaction distribution, not a uniform catalog distribution. Other examples are unobserved candidates, potentially false negatives. Duplicate item columns and known training positives contribute to positive probability mass in the reference loss. This does not remove all false negatives or correct exposure bias. The dense positive mask is practical only for this small dataset; use sparse or indexed membership at scale.

logQ correction concerns the candidate sampling mechanism; it does not solve impression/auction selection bias. Derive Q for the actual batch/mixed sampler, including duplicates and expected counts, before applying a correction. Do not subtract training popularity from inference scores by habit. See Yi and Yang.

Required Phase 2 report

  • [ ] Identical splits, candidates, exclusions, and K across random/popularity/MF/two-tower.
  • [ ] A plain dot-product MF baseline trained with a documented loss; the reference's linear towers are already closely related to MF.
  • [ ] Head/tail groups defined with training counts; report group sizes and cold items.
  • [ ] Light/heavy groups defined with training user counts, not future activity.
  • [ ] Per-user timestamp audit plus the separate global cutoff evaluation.
  • [ ] Several seeds and uncertainty estimates for claims beyond the smoke test.

ANN neighbor overlap and held-out-target Recall@K are distinct: the former asks whether an index approximates exact vector search; the latter asks whether the model retrieves a relevant target. An ANN benchmark over all user embeddings is not a future-query production latency measurement.

These evaluation risks connect to Schnabel et al. (2016).

ann-lab.html:
Read Johnson/FAISS and HNSW first; ScaNN is an optional quantization extension.

python -m pip install -r requirements-ann.txt
python -m src.ann --run artifacts/movielens-v0 --k 100

The runnable reference exports a table to ann.json: Flat exact search, IVF with several nprobe settings, and HNSW with two efSearch values. It measures neighbor overlap against exact top-K, p50/p95 single-query latency, serial QPS, and serialized index bytes. Queries are the first 128 trained user vectors; these are a small reproducible benchmark, not a sampled production workload.

Your implementation tasks

  • [ ] Reimplement Flat indexing and confirm exact-neighbor agreement.
  • [ ] Rebuild IVF and HNSW; explain what each parameter changes.
  • [ ] Plot overlap against p95 latency; add held-out-target recall separately.
  • [ ] Add seen/eligibility filtering and overfetch until K eligible candidates remain.
  • [ ] Measure resident/build memory separately; serialized bytes are only storage size.
  • [ ] Repeat at a larger catalog scale. Label duplicated/synthetic scale tests honestly.
  • [ ] Add a persisted index manifest that carries the exported model hash and item-ID mapping.
  • [ ] Reject an index/user-tower version mismatch in your serving function; test it.

The reference verifies hashes of weights and the paired user/item export before building indexes. This catches accidental file mixing. It is not yet a serving API or an incremental index system. Production manifests also need the feature schema, catalog mapping, preprocessing version, index settings, and build time.

The tiny MovieLens catalog may favor brute force. A slower ANN result here is useful evidence, not a benchmark failure. Normalization makes inner product and cosine ordering equivalent for this model.
